subsections.subsection_title: 30. How to present a NORMAL respiratory examination

blocks.text: “This is a child who is alert and comfortable at rest with no evidence of respiratory distress. The respiratory rate is ___ breaths per minute and oxygen saturation is ___% on room air. There is no nasal flaring, chest recession or cyanosis. The trachea is central and chest expansion is symmetrical. Percussion is resonant bilaterally. Air entry is equal with vesicular breath sounds and there are no added sounds. There is no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy or digital clubbing.”

“The child is tachypnoeic with increased work of breathing. There is reduced expansion of the right lower chest with dullness to percussion and bronchial breath sounds with increased vocal resonance over the right lower zone. There are associated crackles. These findings are consistent with right lower-zone pulmonary consolidation, clinically suggestive of pneumonia.”

content_groups.group_title: Q1. What are signs of respiratory distress?

blocks.text: Tachypnoea, nasal flaring, chest recession, grunting, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, head bobbing in infants, difficulty feeding and altered consciousness.

content_groups.group_title: Q2. Why do you count respiratory rate for one minute?

blocks.text: Because young children may have irregular respiratory patterns, and a full-minute count provides a more accurate measurement.

Q9. What is a silent chest?

blocks.text: Very markedly reduced or absent air movement on auscultation despite severe respiratory distress, classically seen in severe asthma. It is an emergency sign.

content_groups.group_title: Q10. What is the difference between stridor and wheeze?

blocks.text: Stridor is typically a harsh, predominantly inspiratory sound associated with upper airway obstruction, whereas wheeze is usually a musical sound, often expiratory, associated with lower airway narrowing.

content_groups.group_title: 🔥 The findings-to-diagnosis table you should know

blocks.text: **A child with breathing difficulty → first assess severity, then localize the respiratory problem.**
Don't start by thinking “What disease is this?” Start with:
**“Is this child maintaining their airway, ventilation and oxygenation?”**
Then determine whether the findings suggest **upper airway obstruction, lower airway obstruction, consolidation, pleural disease, or another process**.
